We analyzed the laser data as follows. We calculated the wavelength-dependent transmissivity using

$$ \tau_{\lambda}=\frac{T_{\lambda,f}}{T_{\lambda,100}}, $$

where $T_{\lambda,f}$ is the normalized transmission detector signal with the film in place,

$$ T_{\lambda,f}=\frac{J_{\lambda,f}}{J_{\lambda,f,r}}, $$

and $T_{\lambda,100}$ is the normalized transmission detector signal with the film shifted out of the beam path,

$$ T_{\lambda,100}=\frac{J_{\lambda,100}}{J_{\lambda,100,r}}. $$

Here $J$ indicates the current produced by the photodetector and subscript $r$ denotes the reference detector measurement used for normalization of the laser intensity fluctuations.

We calculated the wavelength-dependent reflectivity according to

$$ \varrho_{\lambda}=\frac{R_{\lambda,f}-R_{\lambda,0}}{R_{\lambda,100}-R_{\lambda,0}}. $$

Here, $R_{\lambda,f}$ is the normalized reflection detector signal with the film in place

$$ R_{\lambda,f}=\frac{J_{\lambda,f}}{J_{\lambda,f,r}}, $$

$R_{\lambda,0}$ is the normalized reflection detector signal with the film shifted out of the beam path

$$ R_{\lambda,0}=\frac{J_{\lambda,0}}{J_{\lambda,0,r}}, $$

and $R_{\lambda,100}$ is the normalized reflection detector signal with the \chAu reference chip in place of the film, normalized by the calculated reflectivity for the chip $\varrho_{\lambda,c}$

$$ R_{\lambda,100}=\left(\frac{J_{\lambda,100}}{J_{\lambda,100,r}}\right)\!\left(\frac{1}{\varrho_{\lambda,c}}\right). $$

We estimated a $\pm 3\%$ uncertainty for the reflectivity and transmissivity values, which we applied to each of the three spots that we measured. To obtain the error bars shown in the main article, we determined the maximum and minimum values among the three datasets, e.g., $\tau_{\lambda}^{max}=\text{max}\left(\tau_{\lambda,A}^{+},\tau_{\lambda,B}^{+},\tau_{\lambda,C}^{+}\right)$ or $\varrho_{\lambda}^{min}=\text{min}\left(\varrho_{\lambda,A}^{-},\varrho_{\lambda,B}^{-},\varrho_{\lambda,C}^{-}\right)$ , where here the $+$ and $-$ superscripts indicate the $+3\%$ and $-3\%$ uncertainty values, respectively. We compounded these errors for the absorptivity uncertainty values, e.g., $\alpha_{\lambda}^{max}=1-\tau_{\lambda}^{min}-\varrho_{\lambda}^{min}$ .

Finally, we note that each measurement was made with the laser spot focused in the center of one of the corrugated hexagon areas, rather than on the perimeter of a hexagon near the vertical walls. This was a practical decision on our part in order to simplify the experiments. In a practical light sail, laser light would naturally be incident upon these vertical components, which present a longer path length for absorption than the planar film areas. Here we offer several comments on this. First, any practical sail film must exhibit virtually zero absorption in the Doppler-shifted wavelength range. Though the absorption path length would be roughly two orders of magnitude larger in the vertical components than the planar regions, this difference might be inconsequential compared to extinction coefficients close to zero for both \chAl2O3 and \chMoS2. Second, for the more immediately achievable goal of intra-solar-system light sail travel in which lower laser powers were required, incident photon fluxes on the sail would conceivably not be high enough to cause damage, even in the vertical corrugated components. Third, future research may reveal sail configurations that do not require corrugation to prevent wrinkles; in such cases, a non-corrugated embodiment of our \chAl2O3-\chMoS2-\chAl2O3 sail would still be advantageous due to its low areal density and high reflectivity. Fourth, we have developed an alternative corrugated architecture in which planar \chMoS2 films are wet chemical transferred onto the tops of \chAl2O3-coated trenches (Figure S23) [63]. This implementation reduces the amount of absorbing material in the vertical components, thereby mitigating the risk of excessive absorption there. Finally, detailed simulations should be done to specifically account for the presence of the vertical walls and hexagons (including any diffractive effects) at the small scales employed in this work, which we leave to future work.

## 10 Estimate of optical requirements and thermally-limited power

Here we estimate the required ratio of infrared emissivity to laser band absorptivity for the sail film. We assume to first order that at all points throughout its acceleration, the sail will be in thermal equilibrium such that any energy it absorbs (per unit area) it also must radiate out. We perform this estimate on a per-unit-area basis because the thermal conductivity of nanometer-thick sails will likely be so low that, for curved sails, the center region (perpendicular to the incident laser photons) may be significantly hotter than the perimeter areas [10].

$$ e_{absorb}=e_{radiate} $$

The energy absorbed from the incident laser photons per unit area can be estimated by

$$ e_{absorb}=\frac{\mkern 1.5mu\overline{\mkern-1.5mu\alpha_{\perp}\mkern-1.5mu}\mkern 1.5mu\Phi_{s}}{A_{\perp}} $$

where $\mkern 1.5mu\overline{\mkern-1.5mu\alpha_{\perp}\mkern-1.5mu}\mkern 1.5mu$ is the laser band-average absorptivity (Equation S81), $\Phi_{s}$ is the instantaneous incident photon power hitting the sail, and $A_{\perp}$ is the area of the sail perpendicular to the incident laser beam (Equation S47). The energy radiated per unit area can be estimated by

$$ e_{radiate}=2\varepsilon_{e}\sigma T^{4} $$

where $\varepsilon_{e}$ is the hemispherical effective emissivity of the sail at $T=1000$ $\mathrm{K}$ (Equation S83), $\sigma$ is the Stefan-Boltzmann constant, $T$ is the sail temperature, and the factor of two indicates that radiation can occur from both sides of the sail film. Equating Equations S99 and S100 and solving for the ratio $\frac{\varepsilon_{e}}{\mkern 1.5mu\overline{\mkern-1.5mu\alpha_{\perp}\mkern-1.5mu}\mkern 1.5mu}$ gives

$$ \frac{\varepsilon_{e}}{\mkern 1.5mu\overline{\mkern-1.5mu\alpha_{\perp}\mkern-1.5mu}\mkern 1.5mu}=\frac{\Phi_{s}}{2A_{\perp}\sigma T^{4}}. $$

At a laser power of $\Phi_{s}=100$ $\mathrm{GW}$ (when the $\beta=0$ , the power incident on the sail is equal to the laser output power; see Equation S35), a sail perpendicular-to-laser area of $A_{\perp}=1$ ${\mathrm{m}}^{2}$ , and a reasonable maximum sail temperature of $T=1000$ $\mathrm{K}$ (at which point the sail would likely begin to sublime or melt [14]), the ratio becomes roughly $\frac{\varepsilon_{e}}{\mkern 1.5mu\overline{\mkern-1.5mu\alpha_{\perp}\mkern-1.5mu}\mkern 1.5mu}\approx 10^{6}$ . Since the emissivity of films this thin is likely to be $\varepsilon_{e}\sim 10^{-3}$ , it is essential that the laser band absorptivity be $\mkern 1.5mu\overline{\mkern-1.5mu\alpha_{\perp}\mkern-1.5mu}\mkern 1.5mu\sim 10^{-9}$ , or virtually zero.

Similarly, we can estimate the maximum power that a sail can tolerate, given an emissivity-absorptivity ratio $\frac{\varepsilon_{e}}{\mkern 1.5mu\overline{\mkern-1.5mu\alpha_{\perp}\mkern-1.5mu}\mkern 1.5mu}$ , a maximum material temperature $T_{max}$ , and a perpendicular-to-laser area $A_{\perp}$ .

$$ \Phi_{s,max}=2\frac{\varepsilon_{e}}{\mkern 1.5mu\overline{\mkern-1.5mu\alpha_{\perp}\mkern-1.5mu}\mkern 1.5mu}A_{\perp}\sigma T_{max}^{4} $$

In our calculations, we have used a consistent temperature of $T=1000$ $\mathrm{K}$ to calculate the effective emissivity (Equation S83), although some sails could tolerate higher maximum temperatures before melting or vaporizing. This simplification is reasonable given other uncertainties, such as the temperature dependence of the indices of refraction of the sail materials (see Section 16).

According to Equation S102, sails with higher emissivity-absorptivity ratios can tolerate higher laser power values. In addition, the fourth-order dependence on the material temperature suggests that sails that have higher thermal limits will realize substantial accelerative improvements. Finally, sail films that have lower areal densities can be made to be larger for the same total sail mass, reducing the optical intensity (power per area) at any point on the sail and allowing higher overall laser powers to be used.

## 11 Strength analysis

The photon pressure (Equation S45) experienced by the sail will cause stress and strain in the sail film. For a thin spherically-curved sail with thickness $t_{f}$ and radius of curvature $s_{s}$ experiencing a pressure $P$ , the membrane stress $\sigma_{s}$ can be approximated by [15, 152, 153, 154, 101]

$$ \sigma_{s}=\frac{Ps_{s}}{2t_{f}} $$

*Figure S24: | Schematic diagram of a spherically curved circular sail. The perspective provided is a side view, and the sail is shaded. The sail’s diameter is equal to its spherical radius of curvature: $d_{s}=s_{s}$ .*

(See Figure S24 for an explanation of the sail diameter and radius of curvature.) More complicated analyses can be done for the stress in multilayer nanolaminate films [105, 106], but the simple form above is expedient for analyses in which the uncertainty of many other variables (e.g., the laser power, the sail temperature, the sail’s optical properties, etc.) is relatively large. Rearranging Equation S103 produces

$$ \sigma_{s}t_{f}=\frac{Ps_{s}}{2}, $$

where we define the right side of this expression as the photon-induced tension,

$$ \Upsilon=\frac{Ps_{s}}{2}. $$

This quantity, with dimensions force per unit length, can be thought of as the force acting to create a tear of some length in the sail. At the verge of failure (sail tearing), the membrane stress will be equal to the tensile yield stress $\sigma_{y}$ of the material, i.e., $\sigma_{s}=\sigma_{y}$ . Making this substitution in Equation S104 gives

$$ \sigma_{s}t_{f}=\sigma_{y}t_{f}=\Upsilon. $$

We can extend the left side of Equation S106 to be applicable to composite materials using the rule of mixtures [107, 108, 109]. The rule of mixtures states that the yield stress of a composite film $\sigma_{y,c}$ composed of $n$ layers can be estimated by

$$ \sigma_{y,c}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}f_{i}\sigma_{y,i}, $$

where, if we define the total composite film thickness to be

$$ t_{c}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}t_{f,i} $$

(see also Equation S10), the fractional composition of the $i$ th component can be obtained by

$$ f_{i}=\frac{t_{f,i}}{t_{c}} $$

(see also Equations S12 and S13). Multiplying Equation S107 by $t_{c}$ and simplifying, we obtain

$$ \displaystyle t_{c}\sigma_{y,c} \displaystyle=t_{c}\sum_{i=1}^{n}f_{i}\sigma_{y,i} \displaystyle=t_{c}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{t_{f,i}}{t_{c}}\sigma_{y,i} \displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{n}t_{f,i}\sigma_{y,i}. $$

Equation S110 allows us to calculate the product of the unified composite thickness and its unified tensile yield strength from the thicknesses and yield strengths of its individual layers and materials. We define the right side of this equation as the membrane mechanical robustness,

$$ \wp=\sum_{i=1}^{n}G_{i}t_{f,i}\sigma_{y,i}, $$

where $G_{i}$ are geometrical parameters to account for the presence of holes or other architected features in the film layers, discussed below. Using this result in Equation S106, in our simulations, we defined mechanical failure of the film at the point where

$$ \wp=\Upsilon. $$

The geometrical parameters can be calculated using Equation S113. For films that are planar or have repeating sections that are planar, $G_{i}$ are taken as unity. For periodic films with holes of diameter $d_{hole}$ and period $a_{pattern}$ , $G_{i}$ are the fractional connected lengths.

$$ G_{i}=\begin{cases}1&\mathrm{planar}\\
\frac{a_{pattern}-d_{hole}}{a_{pattern}}&\mathrm{periodic~holes}\end{cases} $$

Finally, for reference, we calculated the membrane mechanical robustness for monolayer graphene to be about 44 $\mathrm{N}\text{${}\!\cdot\!{}$}{\mathrm{m}}^{-1}$ [155], and that for a sheet of standard letter paper to be roughly 3 $\mathrm{kN}\text{${}\!\cdot\!{}$}{\mathrm{m}}^{-1}$ [156].

## 12 Calculation of maximum relative velocity

Here we explain our procedure for calculating the maximum relative velocity achievable by a given film design, $\beta_{max}$ . We will provide specific details about the inputs to this method, such as areal density and laser output wavelength, for each sail film that we evaluated [13, 23, 25, 19, 14, 24, 27], in Section 14.

For a given sail film, we began by using its material thickness, architecture, and yield stress information to calculate its areal density (simply denoted $\rho_{a}$ here) and membrane mechanical robustness $\wp$ (Equation S111). We then used this areal density to calculate the surface area of one side of a spherically curved sail with a mass of $m_{s}=1$ $\mathrm{g}$ :

$$ A_{s}=\frac{m_{s}}{\rho_{a}} $$

Next, we used this area to calculate the diameter $d_{s}$ of a spherically-curved circular sail that has a spherical radius of curvature equal to its diameter, $s_{s}=d_{s}$ . See Figure S24 for an explanation of the sail diameter and radius of curvature.

$$ d_{s}=s_{s}=\sqrt{\frac{A_{s}}{\pi\left(2-\sqrt{3}\right)}} $$

Equation S115 can be derived from Equation S44 in the Supporting Information for Campbell et al. [15] by setting $d_{s}=s_{s}$ . The condition $s_{s}\approx d_{s}$ is optimal for curved light sails [15]. We next used this sail diameter to estimate the maximum distance $L_{max}$ over which the sail could be accelerated with the laser perfectly focused on the full sail area for an Earth-bound laser array diameter $d_{l,E}=30$ $\mathrm{km}$ and a constant laser output wavelength $\lambda_{l}$ [118]:

$$ L_{max}=\frac{d_{l,E}d_{s}}{2\lambda_{l}}. $$

We obtained this expression from Equation S44 in this document. Notice that, given the mass constraint, the sail diameter is inversely proportional to the areal density, which implies sails with higher areal densities have shorter acceleration “runways” $L$ . This is one constraining factor on $\beta_{max}$ .

We next iteratively determined the maximum constant laser output power $\Phi_{l}$ that the sail could sustain without tearing as it accelerated out to a distance $L$ , up to a maximum power of $\Phi_{l}=100$ $\mathrm{GW}$ . We defined the tearing failure mode according to Equation S112, i.e., at the point where the photon-induced tension $\Upsilon$ (Equation S105) would be equal to the film’s membrane mechanical robustness $\wp$ (Equation S111).

$$ \wp=\Upsilon. $$

In this calculation we assumed a total rest sailcraft mass (including sail, payload, and any connecting tethers) of $m_{tot}=2$ $\mathrm{g}$ (i.e., twice the sail mass); having approximately equal sail and payload masses is optimal for acceleration [4, 13, 118, 15].

It is instructive to obtain an expression for the photon-induced tension in terms of the laser power and other sail design parameters. We achieved this by substituting Equation S45 into Equation S105 and simplifying knowing that we chose $d_{s}=s_{s}$ for this analysis. In the following, we also substituted $\Phi_{l,\beta}=\Phi_{l}$ , which states that the output power produced by the laser is constant.

$$ \frac{Ps_{s}}{2}=\Upsilon=\frac{4\varrho_{\beta,\perp}\Phi_{l}}{\pi cd_{s}}\!\left(\frac{1-\beta}{1+\beta}\right). $$

The photon-induced tension is proportional to the film’s laser band reflectivity $\varrho_{\beta,\perp}$ and the constant laser output power $\Phi_{l}$ , and inversely proportional to the sail diameter $d_{s}$ . It also decreases as $\beta$ increases. Since $\varrho_{\beta,\perp}$ and $d_{s}$ are prescribed by the sail design, some films required that the laser power be throttled back to a value lower than 100 $\mathrm{GW}$ . For other films, a power greater than this could be tolerated, in which case we simply applied the maximum power of 100 $\mathrm{GW}$ .

Finally, given the maximum achievable laser power, we stepped through Equation S36 by incrementally increasing the relative velocity $\beta$ until the distance the sail has traveled is equal to $L_{max}$ . We defined the corresponding relative velocity as $\beta_{max}$ .

One may observe that Equation S117, which we use to calculate the maximum power that the sail can sustain without tearing, depends on $\beta$ . Thus, the power iteration step required calculating over a range of $\beta$ values, the upper limit of which was initially an unknown. In practice, we set a high upper limit for $\beta$ and later checked to ensure that, if the laser output power was required to be limited at some $\beta=\beta_{limit}$ , that limit occurred for $\beta_{limit}\leq\beta_{max}$ .

Lastly, note that Equation S117 is based on the perpendicular reflectivity of the sail ( $\varrho_{\beta,\perp}$ ), whereas Equation S36 uses the spatially-averaged reflectivity that accounts for the impact of the sail curvature ( $\varrho_{\beta,a}$ ; see Section 7.2). In in our $\beta_{max}$ calculations, we used the perpendicular reflectivity in place of the average reflectivity. This was because, for many of the sails in Figure 4 of the main article, angle-dependent reflectivity information, necessary for calculating the spatially-averaged reflectivity, was not available. We expect this approximation to slightly inflate the $\beta_{max}$ values calculated for some designs.

## 13 Information on film thickness optimization

We determined the \chAl2O3 and \chMoS2 film thicknesses of our proposed optimized design using the following method. We first selected hexagonal corrugation dimensions that would increase the film’s bending stiffness enhancement factor $\mathbb{B}$ (thereby making the film more resistant to wrinkling) and decrease its tensile stiffness reduction factor $\mathbb{T}$ (thereby making the film more stretchy), as described in Section 3 and illustrated in Figure 3(e) in the main article and Figure S14(a). We chose a hexagon diameter $d_{h}=70~$\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolMicro m}$$ , a trench width $w_{t}=2~$\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolMicro m}$$ , and a trench height $h_{t}=3~$\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolMicro m}$$ . Also, for simplicity, we added the constraint that the top and bottom \chAl2O3 thicknesses should be equal. For optical property information, to determine the best sail accelerative performance within state-of-the-art fabrication capabilities, we used \chAl2O3 index of refraction data from Kischkat et al. [38] and \chMoS2 index of refraction data from Munkhbat et al. [35]. In doing so, we assumed that future process improvements would allow multilayer \chMoS2 films to be fabricated with optical quality equivalent to that of bulk \chMoS2 crystals. Furthermore, we set the sail mass to $m_{s}=1$ $\mathrm{g}$ and the total sailcraft mass (sail with payload chip and any tethers) to be $m_{tot}=2$ $\mathrm{g}$ .

Next, we examined multiple film design combinations spanning \chAl2O3 film thicknesses $\langle 1\leq t_{A,b}=t_{A,t}\leq 100\rangle$ $\mathrm{nm}$ and \chMoS2 film thicknesses $\langle 1\leq t_{M}\leq 200\rangle$ $\mathrm{nm}$ . For each, we calculated the areal density $\rho_{a,c,t}$ (Equations S3, S5, and S7, with $\rho_{A}=3200$ $\mathrm{kg}\text{${}\!\cdot\!{}$}{\mathrm{m}}^{-3}$ [41] and $\rho_{M}=5060$ $\mathrm{kg}\text{${}\!\cdot\!{}$}{\mathrm{m}}^{-3}$ [42]), membrane mechanical robustness $\wp$ (Equation S111 with $G_{i}=1$ and tensile yield stress values $\sigma_{y,\ch{Al2O3}}=2$ $\mathrm{GPa}$ [96, 97] and $\sigma_{y,\ch{MoS2}}=2.3$ $\mathrm{GPa}$ [98]), wavelength-dependent reflectivity within the Doppler-shifted laser band $\varrho_{\beta,\perp}$ (Equation S75), and maximum relative velocity $\beta_{max}$ for a laser array diameter $d_{l,E}=30$ $\mathrm{km}$ and a constant maximum laser output power of $\Phi_{l}=100$ $\mathrm{GW}$ . As discussed in Section 4, the value we used for the \chMoS2 tensile yield stress assumes that future fabrication improvements will allow thick and strong crystalline films to be formed; our estimate is reasonable given comparable data for a similar material, \chMoSe2 [102].

We considered the optimized design to be that which achieved the highest $\beta_{max}$ value. Our model predicted that this design, with \chAl2O3 thickness $t_{A,b}=t_{A,t}\approx 19$ $\mathrm{nm}$ and \chMoS2 thickness $t_{M}\approx 63$ $\mathrm{nm}$ ), will achieve $\beta_{max}=0.26$ . Our proposed optimized film has a corrugated areal density $\rho_{a,c,t}=0.51$ $\mathrm{g}\text{${}\!\cdot\!{}$}{\mathrm{m}}^{-2}$ , a bending stiffness enhancement factor of $\mathbb{B}=890$ , and a tensile stiffness reduction factor of $\mathbb{T}=0.0033$ . We note that the optimization procedure outlined here does not account for thermal constraints. Depending on the extinction coefficients of \chAl2O3 and \chMoS2, thermal considerations might require reducing the laser power to prevent the sail from sublimating, which would consequently decrease $\beta_{max}$ . Such an optimization would be more relevant if reliable spectroscopic data at elevated temperatures for \chAl2O3 and \chMoS2 was available (see Section 16).

Contour plots showing the results of the film thickness optimization are provided in Figure S25. The optimal design (with the highest $\beta_{max}$ value) does not achieve the highest reflectivity within the design space, in part because it decreases its areal density by reducing its \chMoS2 thickness. Notice that, according to Equation S116, the acceleration length $L_{max}$ scales with the sail diameter $d_{s}$ , which depends on the sail area $A_{s}$ (Equation S115), which in turn depends on the areal density $\rho_{a}$ (Equation S114). This explains why the shapes of the contours in Figure S25(f) mirror those of the areal density in panel (b).

## 14 Comparison of films in the literature

### 14.1 Excluded designs

Figure 4 of the main article compares several light sail films introduced in the literature [13, 19, 14, 23, 24, 25, 27]. The data from this figure are presented in Table S2. Other sail designs have been suggested, as well, which we excluded for a variety of reasons. Some were theoretical proposals [20, 26, 15, 10]; others were non-continuous designs where a membrane mechanical robustness $\wp$ was not definable [18, 22]; one was a preliminary design outside the feasible atmospheric transmission wavelength range [21]; and others only reflected strongly at a single wavelength rather than across the entire Doppler-shifted laser wavelength band [17, 16]. A noteworthy design by Norder et al. [28] presented experimentally-measured reflectivity data, but the wavelength range provided ( $\lambda=\langle 1.53,1.62\rangle$ $\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolMicro m}$ ) was too small to allow for a full $\beta_{max}$ simulation ( $\lambda=\langle 1.55,1.8984\rangle$ $\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolMicro m}$ ). Finally, a recent design by Whittam et al. [157] employed a polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) connecting structure that had a low thermal limit (around 600 $\mathrm{K}$ [158]) and a low tensile yield strength (around 5 $\mathrm{MPa}$ [159]), which limited it to low laser powers.

### 14.2 Ilic, Went, and Atwater (2018) [13]

The paper by Ilic, Went, and Atwater [13] contained several silica-based designs and used a laser output wavelength of $\lambda_{l}=1.2$ $\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolMicro m}$ . For comparison, we selected what the paper refers to as design “A11,” which consisted of \chSiO2 layers separated by air/vacuum gaps, due to its high reflectivity and high membrane mechanical robustness (see Table S1 in the Supplementary Information for that paper). We used the design’s layer thicknesses and index of refraction information for \chSiO2 from Rodriguez-de Marcos et al. [78] to calculate the wavelength-dependent reflectivity for this design using the transfer-matrix method (Section 6), which we then averaged to determine the laser band ( $\beta=0$ to $\beta=0.2$ ) average reflectivity $\mkern 1.5mu\overline{\mkern-1.5mu\varrho_{\perp}\mkern-1.5mu}\mkern 1.5mu$ (Equation S78). We used the same data in Equations S80 and S81 to estimate the laser-band-average absorptivity, with fill factors for the layers $F_{i}=1$ since the layers in this design were planar.

We used spectroscopic information from Kischkat et al. [38] and the transfer-matrix method to determine the sail’s spectral directional emissivity in the wavelength range $\lambda=\langle 2,14\rangle$ $\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolMicro m}$ , and subsequently integrated this data at a temperature of $T=1000$ $\mathrm{K}$ to find the film’s effective emissivity $\varepsilon_{e}$ (Equation S83). The wavelength range $\lambda=\langle 2,14\rangle$ $\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolMicro m}$ includes a majority of the emissive power at $T=1000$ $\mathrm{K}$ and conveniently allowed us to make use of the Kischkat et al. [38] datasets for \chAl2O3, \chSi3N4, \chSiO2, and \chTiO2 without extrapolation.

We calculated the membrane mechanical robustness $\wp$ using Equation S111, with geometrical parameters $G_{i}=1$ and yield stress $\sigma_{y,\ch{SiO2}}=1.5$ $\mathrm{GPa}$ [91, 92]. We calculated the areal density $\rho_{a}$ using

$$ \rho_{a}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\rho_{i}t_{f,i} $$

where $\rho_{i}$ and $t_{f,i}$ are the density and thickness of each layer, respectively; in this case $\rho_{\ch{SiO2}}=2030$ $\mathrm{kg}\text{${}\!\cdot\!{}$}{\mathrm{m}}^{-3}$ [87] and $\rho_{gap}=0$ $\mathrm{kg}\text{${}\!\cdot\!{}$}{\mathrm{m}}^{-3}$ (see Table S1). We obtained the maximum relative velocity achievable for this design, $\beta_{max}$ , using the method outlined in Section 12 with the reflectivity profile that we calculated above. Notably, the relatively high membrane mechanical robustness value of this design allowed it to sustain the maximum laser power of $\Phi_{l}=100$ $\mathrm{GW}$ in this simulation. Lastly, we estimated the thermally-limited power $\Phi_{s,max}$ using Equation S102, with $A_{\perp}$ obtained via Equation S47 (using the sail diameter $d_{s}$ derived from the sail’s areal density and a mass of $m_{s}=1$ $\mathrm{g}$ , Equations S114 and S115) and $T_{max}=1450$ $\mathrm{K}$ (limited by \chSiO2).

### 14.3 Salary and Mosallaei (2020) [19]

The paper by Salary and Mosallaei [19] proposed designs that featured protruding \chSi disks of differing diameters on top of a continuous \chSi-\chSiO2 backbone film, and used a laser output wavelength of $\lambda_{l}=1.3$ $\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolMicro m}$ . For simplicity, we used the reflectivity information contained in Figure 2(b) of their paper [19] with a constant disk diameter of 300 $\mathrm{nm}$ , which we averaged to estimate the mean laser band reflectivity $\mkern 1.5mu\overline{\mkern-1.5mu\varrho_{\perp}\mkern-1.5mu}\mkern 1.5mu$ (Equation S78).

We estimated the absorptivity using Equations S80 and S81 with optical data from Poruba et al. [77] and Rodriguez-de Marcos et al. [78] for \chSi and \chSiO2, respectively. We accounted for the protruding \chSi disks using fill factor

$$ F_{i}=\frac{\pi\left(\frac{d_{disk}}{2}\right)^{2}}{a^{2}}, $$

where $d_{disk}$ is the protruding disk diameter and $a$ is the period of the pattern, and used a fill factor $F_{i}=1$ for the connecting (continuous) 89- $\mathrm{nm}$ -thick \chSi and 60- $\mathrm{nm}$ -thick \chSiO2 layers below.

We calculated the sail’s emissivity as in Section 14.2, using optical data from Franta et al. [79] and Kischkat et al. [38] for \chSi and \chSiO2, respectively, along with an effective medium approximation [160]. We calculated the membrane mechanical robustness using Equation S111 with $G_{i}=1$ , accounting only for the strength of the backbone \chSi-\chSiO2 film (not the \chSi disks), with yield stress values $\sigma_{y,\ch{Si}}=2$ $\mathrm{GPa}$ [89, 90, 93, 95] and $\sigma_{y,\ch{SiO2}}=1.5$ $\mathrm{GPa}$ [91, 92]. We estimated the sail’s areal density by averaging the two extreme areal density values given in the paper [19] for the largest and smallest protruding \chSi disks. We calculated the sail’s maximum relative velocity using the method outlined in Section 12 with the reflectivity profile obtained from Figure 2(b) of their paper [19] as discussed above. Lastly, we estimated the thermally-limited power $\Phi_{s,max}$ as in Section 14.2, using $T_{max}=1450$ $\mathrm{K}$ (limited by \chSiO2).

### 14.4 Brewer et al. (2022) [14]

Brewer et al. [14] proposed a three-layer \chSi3N4-\chMoS2-\chSi3N4 composite film (thicknesses $t_{\ch{Si3N4},t}=5$ $\mathrm{nm}$ , $t_{\ch{MoS2}}=90$ $\mathrm{nm}$ , and $t_{\ch{Si3N4},b}=5$ $\mathrm{nm}$ ) with patterned holes (diameter $d_{hole}=1044$ $\mathrm{nm}$ , $x$ -period $a_{x}=2009$ $\mathrm{nm}$ , and $y$ -period $a_{y}=1160$ $\mathrm{nm}$ ). We averaged the reflectivity information provided in Figure 2(c) of their paper [14] to find the mean laser band reflectivity $\mkern 1.5mu\overline{\mkern-1.5mu\varrho_{\perp}\mkern-1.5mu}\mkern 1.5mu$ (Equation S78), and used Equations S80 and S81 with spectroscopic data from Kischkat et al. [38] and Munkhbat et al. [35] for \chSi3N4 and \chMoS2, respectively, to estimate the average absorptivity. We accounted for the holes in the sail film in Equation S80 using fill factor

$$ F_{i}=\frac{a_{x}a_{y}-2\pi\left(\frac{d_{hole}}{2}\right)^{2}}{a_{x}a_{y}}, $$

where the factor of two in front of $\pi$ is included because each unit cell in their design contained the equivalent of two holes. We obtained the effective emissivity as in Section 14.2 using spectroscopic data from Kischkat et al. [38] and Munkhbat et al. [35] for \chSi3N4 and \chMoS2, respectively.

We derived the sail’s membrane mechanical robustness using Equation S111 with

$$ G_{i}=\frac{a_{y}-d_{hole}}{a_{y}} $$

(see Equation S113) and yield stress values $\sigma_{y,\ch{Si3N4}}=14$ $\mathrm{GPa}$ [92] and $\sigma_{y,\ch{MoS2}}=0.75$ $\mathrm{GPa}$ [42, 100]. We calculated the areal density of the film using the ratio of the unit cell mass to the unit cell planar area, i.e.,

$$ \rho_{a}=\frac{M_{uc}}{A_{uc}}, $$

wherein

$$ \displaystyle M_{uc} \displaystyle=\left(\rho_{\ch{Si3N4}}\left(t_{\ch{Si3N4},t}+t_{\ch{Si3N4},b}\right)+\rho_{\ch{MoS2}}t_{\ch{MoS2}}\right) \displaystyle\;\;\;\;\;\;\times\left(a_{x}a_{y}-2\pi\left(\frac{d_{hole}}{2}\right)^{2}\right) $$

and

$$ A_{uc}=a_{y}a_{x}. $$

Here, $\rho_{\ch{Si3N4}}=3200$ $\mathrm{kg}\text{${}\!\cdot\!{}$}{\mathrm{m}}^{-3}$ [86] and $\rho_{\ch{MoS2}}=5060$ $\mathrm{kg}\text{${}\!\cdot\!{}$}{\mathrm{m}}^{-3}$ [42]. As above, the factor of two in front of $\pi$ is included because each unit cell in their design contained the equivalent of two holes. We computed the sail’s maximum relative velocity using the method outlined in Section 12 with the reflectivity profile shown in Figure 2(c) of their paper [14]. In this simulation, we reduced the laser power because the mechanical robustness of the sail was low. Finally, we estimated the thermally-limited power $\Phi_{s,max}$ as in Section 14.2, using $T_{max}=1000$ $\mathrm{K}$ (limited by \chMoS2).

### 14.5 Lien et al. (2022) [23]

Lien et al. [23] fabricated a silicon nitride photonic crystal film by patterning a $t_{\ch{Si3N4}}=690$ $\mathrm{nm}$ thick \chSi3N4 layer with $d_{hole}=415$ $\mathrm{nm}$ holes in a square grid with spacing $a=1064$ $\mathrm{nm}$ . They optimized their design for a laser wavelength of $\lambda_{l}=1.064$ $\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolMicro m}$ and measured the transmissivity of their prototype; assuming negligible absorption, they estimated the reflectivity by subtracting the transmissivity from unity (see Figure 2(c) of their paper [23]). We used this definition of reflectivity to estimate the average laser band reflectivity $\mkern 1.5mu\overline{\mkern-1.5mu\varrho_{\perp}\mkern-1.5mu}\mkern 1.5mu$ for their design (Equation S78).

We used optical data from Kischkat et al. [38] in Equations S80 and S81 to calculate the average laser band absorptivity, and used the method of Section 14.2 to obtain the effective emissivity. We calculated the appropriate fill factor for the absorptivity calculation using

$$ F_{i}=\frac{a_{x}a_{y}-\pi\left(\frac{d_{hole}}{2}\right)^{2}}{a_{x}a_{y}}, $$

where unlike Equation S123, the pattern in the design contained only one hole per unit cell.

We derived the sail’s membrane mechanical robustness using

$$ G_{i}=\frac{a-d_{hole}}{a} $$

(see Equation S113; for this single-layer film $i=1$ only) and yield stress $\sigma_{y,\ch{Si3N4}}=14$ $\mathrm{GPa}$ [92] in Equation S111. We calculated the areal density using Equation S122, with

$$ M_{uc}=\rho_{\ch{Si3N4}}t_{\ch{Si3N4}}\!\left(a^{2}-\pi\left(\frac{d_{hole}}{2}\right)^{2}\right) $$

and

$$ A_{uc}=a^{2}. $$

Here $\rho_{\ch{Si3N4}}=3200$ $\mathrm{kg}\text{${}\!\cdot\!{}$}{\mathrm{m}}^{-3}$ [86] and as mentioned above the pattern in the design contained only one hole per unit cell. We computed the sail’s maximum relative velocity using the method outlined in Section 12 with the reflectivity profile reported in Figure 2(c) of their paper [23]. Finally, we estimated the thermally-limited power $\Phi_{s,max}$ as in Section 14.2, using $T_{max}=1670$ $\mathrm{K}$ (limited by \chSi3N4).

### 14.9 Fabricated prototype film (this study)

The fabricated prototype film characterized in Figure 3(c) of the main article consists of a \chAl2O3-\chMoS2-\chAl2O3 composite ( $t_{A,b}\approx 21~$\mathrm{nm}$$ (bottom \chAl2O3 thickness), $t_{M}\approx 53~$\mathrm{nm}$$ (\chMoS2), $t_{A,t}\approx 51~$\mathrm{nm}$$ (top \chAl2O3)) with a hexagonally corrugated indented trench structure ( $d_{h}\approx 77~$\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolMicro m}$$ , $w_{t}\approx 15~$\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolMicro m}$$ , $h_{t}\approx 10~$\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolMicro m}$$ ; see Figure S11). We averaged our measured reflectivity and absorptivity data $(\alpha_{\lambda,\perp}=1-\varrho_{\lambda,\perp}-\tau_{\lambda,\perp})$ to obtain the laser band average values ( $\beta=0$ to $\beta=0.2$ , or equivalently for our laser wavelength, $\lambda=\langle 1.2,1.4697\rangle$ $\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolMicro m}$ ) for reflectivity $\mkern 1.5mu\overline{\mkern-1.5mu\varrho_{\perp}\mkern-1.5mu}\mkern 1.5mu$ and absorptivity $\mkern 1.5mu\overline{\mkern-1.5mu\alpha_{\perp}\mkern-1.5mu}\mkern 1.5mu$ (Equations S78 and S81, respectively). We used spectroscopic information from Kischkat et al. [38] for \chAl2O3 and a two-term Cauchy expansion of our experimentally-measured \chMoS2 index of refraction (see Figure S18) to estimate the film’s effective emissivity, as in Section 14.2. We calculated the membrane mechanical robustness of our design using Equation S111 with $G_{i}=1$ and yield stress values $\sigma_{y,\ch{Al2O3}}=2$ $\mathrm{GPa}$ [96, 97] and $\sigma_{y,\ch{MoS2}}=0.75$ $\mathrm{GPa}$ [42, 100]. Our choice of $G=1$ is conservative and allows us to examine the robustness of the film in a planar (non-corrugated) state. However, the hexagonal structure can actually be designed to increase compliance to in-plane stresses, thereby increasing the practical membrane mechanical robustness [44]. We derived the areal density using Equations S3, S5, and S7, with $\rho_{A}=3200$ $\mathrm{kg}\text{${}\!\cdot\!{}$}{\mathrm{m}}^{-3}$ [41] and $\rho_{M}=5060$ $\mathrm{kg}\text{${}\!\cdot\!{}$}{\mathrm{m}}^{-3}$ [42]. We calculated the film’s maximum relative velocity using the method outlined in Section 12 using our measured reflectivity data. Finally, we estimated the thermally-limited power $\Phi_{s,max}$ as in Section 14.2, using $T_{max}=1000$ $\mathrm{K}$ (limited by \chMoS2).

The optimized film that we propose consists of a \chAl2O3-\chMoS2-\chAl2O3 composite ( $t_{A,b}\approx 19~$\mathrm{nm}$$ (bottom \chAl2O3 thickness), $t_{M}\approx 63~$\mathrm{nm}$$ (\chMoS2), $t_{A,t}\approx 19~$\mathrm{nm}$$ (top \chAl2O3)) with a hexagonally corrugated indented trench structure ( $d_{h}=70~$\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolMicro m}$$ , $w_{t}=2~$\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolMicro m}$$ , $h_{t}=3~$\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolMicro m}$$ ; see Figure S11). Finally, we estimated the thermally-limited power $\Phi_{s,max}$ as in Section 14.2, using $T_{max}=1000$ $\mathrm{K}$ (limited by \chMoS2).

## 15 Energy analysis of accelerating sail

Here we describe our calculation of the equilibrium temperature during the acceleration of our optimized design. We performed this simulation with similar constraints to the others in this work: a sail mass of $m_{s}=1$ $\mathrm{g}$ , a total sailcraft mass (sail, chip, and tethers) of $m_{tot}=2$ $\mathrm{g}$ , a circular sail with a spherical radius of curvature equal to its diameter $(d_{s}=s_{s})$ , and a maximum constant laser output power of $\Phi_{l}=100$ $\mathrm{GW}$ . Our approach was to divide the acceleration interval ( $\beta=0$ to $\beta=\beta_{f}=0.2$ ) into discrete $\beta$ steps and solve Equation S46 to determine the sail temperature at each relative velocity value. We also checked the mechanical integrity of the sail (photon-induced tension) during its acceleration, using the same material properties as in Section 13.

For the optical properties of \chMoS2 we used the data of Munkhbat et al. [35], extrapolating the $n$ values using a Cauchy expansion and setting the $\kappa$ values equal to $10^{-8}$ at wavelengths equal to and longer than the laser wavelength of $\lambda_{l}=1.2$ $\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolMicro m}$ . For the $n$ optical coefficients of \chAl2O3 we used the data of Querry [37] at all wavelengths. For the $\kappa$ data of \chAl2O3, at wavelengths equal to and shorter than $\lambda_{A}=7$ $\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolMicro m}$ we used the values of Lingart, Petrov, and Tikhonova [36]; at wavelengths equal to and greater than $\lambda_{B}=10$ $\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolMicro m}$ we used the values of Querry [37]; and in between we used a power-law interpolation of the form

$$ \kappa=a\lambda^{b} $$

where

$$ b=\frac{\ln\left(\frac{\kappa_{A}}{\kappa_{B}}\right)}{\ln\left(\frac{\lambda_{A}}{\lambda_{B}}\right)} $$

and

$$ a=\frac{\kappa_{A}}{\lambda_{A}^{b}}. $$

Here, $\kappa_{A}$ and $\kappa_{B}$ correspond to the extinction coefficients provided by Lingart, Petrov, and Tikhonova [36] and Querry [37] at $\lambda_{A}$ and $\lambda_{B}$ , respectively. We used these optical coefficients and the transfer-matrix method to calculate the reflectivity and absorptivity at each $\beta$ -step throughout the acceleration, and also used the transfer-matrix method to obtain the spectral hemispherical emissivity in the wavelength range $\lambda=\langle 0.301,20\rangle$ $\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolMicro m}$ (Equation S82). Also, in order to provide a more realistic portrait of the sail’s accelerative performance, we accounted for the impact of the spherically-curved sail’s shape on its reflectivity using Equation S76, which required calculating angle-dependent reflectivity values.

The results of our calculations are provided in Figure S26. Panel (h) shows that the peak temperature occurred at the beginning of the acceleration phase, and that, even with a laser output power of $\Phi_{l}=100$ $\mathrm{GW}$ , the sail stayed cooler than than the \chMoS2 vacuum sublimation point of about 1000 $\mathrm{K}$ [48]. This result is predicated on our selection of $\kappa=10^{-8}$ for \chMoS2 in the laser band; higher extinction coefficients would require reducing the laser output power to avoid overheating the sail. In this particular simulation, the constraining parameter for this design was the photon-induced tension (panel (g)), which was the factor for which we optimized this design (see Section 13).

A few more aspects of these acceleration calculations are worth discussing. Though we held the laser output power, shown in Figure S26(c), constant, the power incident on the sail decreased with time due to the red shift of the photons and the reduced photon flux relative to the accelerating sail. Notice that the time duration during which the laser needed to produce photons, $t_{l}=5.0$ $\mathrm{min}$ , was less than the sail’s acceleration time, $t_{a}=5.6$ $\mathrm{min}$ , because the last photon leaving the laser took about 0.6 $\mathrm{min}$ to reach the sail. The acceleration experienced by the sail (in its own reference frame) was also higher than that in the laser’s reference frame due to the relativistic increase in the sailcraft’s mass from the laser’s perspective (panel (e)). The average reflectivity of the spherically curved sail (panel (i)) was smaller than that of the perpendicular component (at the sail center); both decreased with time as the laser wavelength reaching the sail (panel (b)) was redshifted. Ultimately, our calculations indicated that our proposed optimized film could accelerate from rest to $\beta=0.2$ over a distance of $L\approx 11$ $\mathrm{Gm}$ , and would require a laser array diameter on Earth of $d_{l,E}\approx 17$ $\mathrm{km}$ .

Our use of an extinction coefficient of $\kappa=10^{-8}$ for \chMoS2 is optimistic but not unreasonable. For instance, Ermolaev et al. [30], Hsu et al. [130], and Liu et al. [131] reported optical coefficients of $\kappa=0$ for \chMoS2 at or near $\lambda=1.2$ $\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolMicro m}$ . We anticipate that future fabrication improvements will allow perfect \chMoS2 sheets to be conformally fabricated over large areas. Our use of the extinction coefficients of Lingart, Petrov, and Tikhonova [36] in the laser wavelength range is done knowing that, if the \chAl2O3 was amorphous as deposited using atomic layer deposition (ALD), it would need to be annealed so it would adopt a crystalline form. Recent work has shown that annealing ALD \chAl2O3 films for just 30 $\mathrm{min}$ in a \chH2 or \chN2 atmosphere at a pressure of $10^{5}$ $\mathrm{Pa}$ and a temperature of around 1000 $\mathrm{K}$ is sufficient to accomplish this [161, 162] (but note that another study suggested a temperature of around 1400 $\mathrm{K}$ [163]). (We also note that, while annealing greatly reduces the extinction coefficient of \chAl2O3, it has only a small impact its real component of the index of refraction [164].) Annealing the alumina may impact its mechanical properties; the yield stress of bulk sapphire is roughly an order of magnitude lower than that for thin ALD alumina films. We are unaware of studies on the mechanical properties of thin sapphire films, but there is some evidence that annealing \chAl2O3 films at temperatures up to 1000 $\mathrm{K}$ does not adversely impact them [165]. Annealing of the face alumina films would need to take place in the presence of the inner \chMoS2 film. As we noted earlier, \chMoS2 is known to sublimate in vacuum environments at temperatures exceeding 1000 $\mathrm{K}$ . However, recent work suggests that it can be heated to 1500 $\mathrm{K}$ without evaporating if it is pressurized to $>100$ $\mathrm{Pa}$ (gaseous environment) [48]. Even if sublimation were to occur, it may be relatively slow; a study by Lu et al. found that at 923 $\mathrm{K}$ and 1300 $\mathrm{Pa}$ it took 1 $\mathrm{h}$ to remove one layer (about 0.65 $\mathrm{nm}$ ) of a \chMoS2 flake [166]. Together, these factors suggest that future \chAl2O3-\chMoS2-\chAl2O3 light sails could feature alumina and \chMoS2 extinction coefficients as low as or even lower than $\kappa=10^{-7}$ and $\kappa=10^{-8}$ , respectively.

## 16 Impact of temperature

Elevated temperatures will impact the mechanical and optical properties of the sail. While a dedicated study of these effects for thin films will ultimately be required (but is now beyond the scope of this work), we can make some observations from related studies in the literature [49].

The mechanical properties of \chAl2O3 and \chMoS2 will degrade with temperature. The fracture stress of sapphire has been found to decrease by roughly 15% from room temperature to 1000 $\mathrm{K}$ [167], and the yield stress of polycrystalline alumina was found to decrease by as much as 62% over the same range [168]. Likewise, molecular dynamics simulations of monolayer \chMoS2 flakes suggest that their ultimate stress decreases by roughly 23% from room temperature to 600 $\mathrm{K}$ [169]. This degradation could be offset by using lower laser powers (decreasing the photon flux and hence the photon-induced tension) or thicker film layers (increasing the sail’s membrane mechanical robustness).

The extinction coefficients for \chAl2O3 and \chMoS2 will likely increase with temperature; unfortunately, high-temperature optical data within the laser band for these materials is scarce. Lingart, Petrov, and Tikhonova [36] compiled information for sapphire at elevated temperatures, which suggests that its extinction coefficient in the laser band roughly triples (190% increase) from room temperature to 1000 $\mathrm{K}$ (Figure S27). However, this is accompanied by a similar increase at longer wavelengths, suggesting that the sail will be able to emit more radiation to slightly offset the increased photon absorption. The real component of the index of refraction of sapphire increases negligibly (1%) over the same temperature range. Data reported by Liu et al. for \chMoS2 suggest that its extinction coefficient in the laser band does not change significantly from 4.5 $\mathrm{K}$ to 300 $\mathrm{K}$ , and that it may decrease at higher temperatures [131] (Figure S28). Also, according to their results, the real component of the index of refraction of \chMoS2 changes by less than 1% from room temperature to 500 $\mathrm{K}$ .

Finally, thermal expansion effects will impact the sail. As shown in Figure S29, \chAl2O3 and \chMoS2 have well-matched thermal expansion coefficients, $\alpha_{A}$ and $\alpha_{M}$ , respectively - within about 5% in the range 500-800 $\mathrm{K}$ and within 10-15% up to 1000 $\mathrm{K}$ [170, 171, 172, 173]. We can estimate the strain $\epsilon_{T}$ that this thermal expansion induces using

$$ \epsilon_{T}=(T-T_{0})\left|\alpha_{A}-\alpha_{M}\right| $$

where $T$ is the temperature of interest and $T_{0}$ is a reference temperature at which the strain is negligible. This equation indicates that the thermal strain will be less than a tenth of a percent from room temperature up to 1000 $\mathrm{K}$ , and therefore suggests that thermal strain is not likely to be a failure mode for the sail.
